p.src: The story tells how the Great Sage Sun accompanied the attending eunuch into the inner palace and stopped outside the door of the royal bedchamber. He handed three golden threads to the eunuch to take inside and instructed him, “Have one of the consorts or an attending eunuch first tie them beneath His Majesty’s left wrist, over the three pulse positions of cun, guan, and chi, then pass the loose ends out to me through the window lattice.” The eunuch did exactly as instructed: he asked the king to sit upon the dragon bed, tied one end of each golden thread over the cun, guan, and chi positions, and drew the other ends out through the window. Pilgrim took the thread ends and, first supporting his forefinger with the thumb of his right hand, examined the cun pulse; next he pressed his middle finger against his thumb and examined the guan pulse; then he supported his ring finger with his thumb and examined the chi pulse. Steadying his own breathing, he distinguished the four qi, five constraints, seven exterior signs, eight interior signs, nine indicators, the floating within the middle and deep, and the floating within the deep, clearly discerning every aspect of deficiency and excess. He then had the threads untied from the left hand and fastened as before beneath the right wrist. Pilgrim examined each pulse in turn with the fingers of his left hand; when he had finished, he gave his body a shake and drew the golden threads onto himself. He cried in a stern, loud voice, “Your Majesty’s left cun pulse is forceful and tight, the guan pulse rough and slow, and the chi pulse hollow and deep; the right cun pulse is floating and slippery, the guan pulse slow and knotted, and the chi pulse rapid and firm. A forceful and tight left cun pulse signifies internal deficiency and heart pain; a rough and slow guan pulse signifies sweating and numbness of the flesh; a hollow and deep chi pulse signifies red urine and blood in the stool. A floating and slippery right cun pulse signifies an internal obstruction and blocked channels; a slow and knotted guan pulse signifies retained food and accumulated fluids; a rapid and firm chi pulse signifies distress and fullness, with deficiency and cold contending against each other. From my examination, Your Majesty’s illness arises from fright, fear, anxiety, and brooding; it is known as the affliction of ‘Two Birds Separated from the Flock.’” Hearing this from within, the king was overjoyed. Rousing himself, he replied loudly, “Your diagnosis is perfectly clear! Perfectly clear! That is indeed my illness. Please go outside and prepare the medicine.”

p.src: Only then did the Great Sage walk slowly out of the palace. A eunuch who had overheard everything had already gone ahead and informed the assembled officials. Presently Pilgrim emerged, and the Tang Monk at once asked how matters stood. Pilgrim said, “I have taken his pulse. Now I shall prepare medicine for the ailment.” The officials came forward and asked, “Reverend divine monk, you just spoke of the affliction of ‘Two Birds Separated from the Flock.’ What does that mean?” Pilgrim laughed and said, “There were once two birds, male and female, that always flew together. Suddenly a violent storm frightened them apart. The female could not see the male, nor the male the female; she yearned for him, and he yearned for her. Is that not ‘Two Birds Separated from the Flock’?” On hearing this, all the officials cheered in unison, “He truly is a divine monk! He truly is a divine physician!” Their praises continued without end. Then an imperial physician asked, “The nature of the illness is now known, but what medicine will you use to cure it?” Pilgrim replied, “There is no need to adhere to a fixed prescription. I shall take whatever medicines I see.” The physician said, “The classics state, ‘There are eight hundred and eight medicines, and four hundred and four human ailments.’ Not every illness exists in a single person, so how could there be any reason to use every medicine? How can you say that you will take whatever medicines you see?” Pilgrim said, “The ancients said, ‘Do not be bound by a prescription; use medicines as circumstances require.’ That is why I shall requisition every kind of medicine, then add or subtract ingredients as I see fit.”

p.src: The physician said no more. He went out through the court gate and ordered the officers on duty in his bureau to notify every shop in the city that sold prepared or crude medicines and procure the ingredients at once. They were to prepare three jin of every kind and deliver them to Pilgrim. Pilgrim said, “This is no place to prepare medicine. Send the full quantity of every drug, together with all the necessary implements, to the Court of Interpreters, and have my two junior disciples receive them.” Obeying him, the physician sent all eight hundred and eight medicines, three jin of each, along with drug rollers, mills, sieves, grinding bowls, mortars, pestles, and similar implements to the hostel, where every item was duly handed over and received.

p.src: Pilgrim went to the hall to ask his master to return with him to the hostel and prepare the medicine. Just as the elder rose, a decree arrived from the inner palace ordering the ministers to detain the Master and lodge him in the Hall of Literary Splendor. After the king had taken the medicine the next morning and recovered, he would reward them, exchange their travel document, and send them on their way. Tripitaka exclaimed in alarm, “Disciple, this means they are keeping me here as a hostage! If you cure him, they will gladly reward us and see us off; but if you fail, my life is over. You must take the greatest care and prepare the medicine with perfect devotion.” Pilgrim laughed. “Master, set your mind at ease and enjoy yourself here. Old Sun possesses the skill to heal a kingdom.”

p.src: Our fine Great Sage took leave of Tripitaka and the assembled ministers and went straight back to the hostel. Bajie came to meet him and said with a laugh, “Brother, I know what you are up to.” “What do you know?” Pilgrim asked. Bajie said, “I know that our scripture pilgrimage has come to nothing and that, having no capital with which to earn a living, you saw how wealthy this place was today and devised a scheme to open an apothecary.” Pilgrim barked, “Stop talking nonsense! Once the king is cured, we shall take our leave of the court in triumph and continue our journey. Why would I open an apothecary?” Bajie said, “Surely not! Eight hundred and eight medicines, three jin of each, make two thousand four hundred and twenty-four jin altogether. How much can you possibly use to treat a single man? Who knows how many years it would take him to swallow it all?” Pilgrim said, “How could I possibly use so much? Those officials of the Imperial Medical Bureau are all ignorant fools. I demanded so many medicines to leave them completely bewildered, unable to discover which few ingredients I actually use or fathom my wondrous prescription.”

p.src: While they were speaking, the two hostel officers came and knelt before them, saying, “We invite the venerable divine monk to partake of the evening vegetarian meal.” Pilgrim said, “You treated me very differently this morning. Why do you now kneel to invite me?” The hostel officers kowtowed and said, “When Your Reverence arrived, we lowly officials had eyes but failed to recognize your honored person. We now hear that Your Reverence has displayed the seasoned skill of an accomplished physician and is treating the sovereign of our whole realm. If His Majesty recovers, Your Reverence will have a share in the kingdom, and we shall all be your subjects; it is therefore proper that we kneel to invite you.” Pleased by these words, Pilgrim entered the hall and took the seat of honor; Bajie and Friar Sand sat on his left and right. When the vegetarian meal had been laid out, Friar Sand asked, “Brother, where is Master?” Pilgrim laughed and said, “The king has detained Master as a hostage. Only after the illness has been cured will he reward us and send us on our way.” Friar Sand asked again, “Is he at least being treated well?” Pilgrim replied, “How could there be any lack of comfort in the king’s palace? When I left, three senior ministers were already attending him and inviting him into the Hall of Literary Splendor.” Bajie said, “Then Master still ranks above us: he has senior ministers attending him, while we have only two hostel officers flattering us. Never mind him for now; let old Hog eat his fill.” The three brothers then enjoyed the meal at their leisure.

p.src: By then it was already late. Pilgrim told the hostel officers, “Clear away the tableware and provide plenty of oil and candles. We can prepare the medicine properly only when the night is quiet.” The hostel officers duly delivered a good quantity of oil and candles, after which Pilgrim dismissed them all.

p.src: By midnight, the streets beneath heaven were still, and not a sound could be heard. Bajie said, “Brother, what medicine are you making? Let us finish the work early; I am getting sleepy.” The Pilgrim said, “Fetch me one liang of rhubarb root and grind it into a fine powder.” Sha the Monk said, “Rhubarb is bitter in taste, cold in nature, and nonpoisonous. Its nature is to sink rather than rise, and its action is to move rather than remain. It sweeps away every congestion without causing obstruction and quells disorder to restore peace. That is why it is called the ‘General.’ It is a powerful purgative, but I fear it should not be used on one weakened by long illness.” The Pilgrim laughed. “Worthy brother, you do not understand. This medicine clears phlegm, regulates the breath, and purges congealed cold and heat from the belly. Never mind what I am doing. Go and fetch one liang of croton seeds, remove their shells and membranes, pound out their poisonous oil, and grind them into a fine powder.” Bajie said, “Croton is pungent in taste, hot in nature, and poisonous. It breaks down hardened accumulations and sweeps deep-seated cold from the lungs and bowels; it opens blockages and clears the passages for water and grain. It is a general who smashes through barriers and seizes gates, and must not be used lightly.” The Pilgrim said, “Worthy brother, you do not understand either. This medicine breaks up obstructions, clears the bowels, and can treat fullness in the chest and swelling from retained water. Make it quickly. I have another ingredient to moderate and assist it.”

p.src: The two of them at once ground the two drugs finely and asked, “Elder Brother, which of the other dozens of ingredients will you use?” The Pilgrim said, “None of them.” Bajie said, “Eight hundred and eight ingredients, three jin of each, yet you use only these two liang! You truly know how to fool people.” The Pilgrim produced a decorated porcelain cup and said, “Worthy brother, enough talk. Take this cup and scrape half a cupful of soot from the underside of the cooking pot.” Bajie asked, “What for?” The Pilgrim said, “It must go into the medicine.” Sha the Monk said, “I have never seen pot soot used in medicine.” The Pilgrim said, “Pot soot is called ‘Frost of a Hundred Herbs.’ It can treat a hundred illnesses. You simply did not know.” The fool obediently scraped off half a cupful and ground it fine as well.

p.src: The Pilgrim handed him the cup again and said, “Now go and collect half a cupful of our horse’s urine.” Bajie asked, “What do you want that for?” The Pilgrim said, “To bind the pills.” Sha the Monk laughed again. “Brother, this is no joking matter. Horse urine reeks so strongly—how could it be used in a medicine? I have only ever seen pills bound with vinegar paste, aged-rice paste, refined honey, or simply clear water. Who has ever seen horse urine used to make pills? That stuff is rank and foul; anyone with a weak spleen would vomit at the first whiff. And if he then takes croton and rhubarb, he will be vomiting and purging at once. Is that a thing to jest about?” The Pilgrim said, “You do not know the truth of it. That horse of mine is no ordinary horse. He was originally a dragon of the Western Sea. If only he can be persuaded to relieve himself, no matter what the illness, a dose of it will cure the patient at once. The difficulty is that it cannot be obtained on demand.” Hearing this, Bajie went straight to the horse, which was lying on its side asleep. The fool kicked it to its feet, crouched beneath its belly, and waited a good while, but not a drop of urine appeared. He ran back and said to the Pilgrim, “Brother, never mind curing the king for now. Hurry and cure the horse first. The wretch is completely stopped up; do not expect to get a single drop from him.” The Pilgrim laughed. “I will go with you.” Sha the Monk said, “I will come and see too.”

p.src: When all three reached the horse, it sprang up, spoke in a human voice, and cried sternly, “Elder Brother, surely you know! I was once a flying dragon of the Western Sea. Because I violated a law of Heaven, the Bodhisattva Guanyin saved me, sawed off my horns, stripped away my scales, and transformed me into a horse to carry our master to the Western Heaven for the scriptures, so that I might atone for my crime through meritorious service. If I urinate while crossing water, any fish that drinks it will become a dragon. If I urinate while crossing a mountain, the grasses there will absorb its essence and turn into magic lingzhi; when immortal lads gather them, they will gain long life. How could I be willing to squander it here in this vulgar mortal place?” The Pilgrim said, “Brother, mind your words. The man here is the king of a western realm, no common mortal, and your gift will not be lightly wasted. As the saying goes, ‘Many hairs gathered together make a fur coat.’ We need it to cure the king of this country. If we cure him, it will bring honor to us all. If not, I fear none of us may leave this place safely.” Only then did the horse call out, “Wait.” Watch how he lunged forward, squatted back, and clenched his teeth until they ground loudly; with tremendous effort he squeezed out only a few drops, then stood upright again. Bajie said, “You wretch! Even if it is liquid gold, you could still give us a little more.” Seeing that there was almost half a cupful, the Pilgrim said, “That is enough, enough. Take it away.” Only then was Sha the Monk pleased.

p.src: The three returned to the hall, mixed all the ingredients together, and rolled them into three large pills. The Pilgrim said, “Brother, they are far too large.” Bajie said, “They are only the size of walnuts. If I were eating them, one would not even make a mouthful.” They then put the pills away in a small box, and the brothers lay down to sleep in their clothes. Nothing more happened that night, and before long dawn arrived.

p.src: Now the king, who had suspended court because of his illness, received Tang Sanzang and immediately ordered the assembled officials to hurry to the guest lodge, pay their respects to the holy monk Elder Sun, and collect the medicine.

p.src: The officials came to the lodge, prostrated themselves before the Pilgrim, and said, “Our king has specially commanded us to receive the wondrous medicine with due reverence.” The Pilgrim told Bajie to fetch the box, opened its lid, and handed it to the officials. The officials respectfully asked, “What is this medicine called? We should know what to tell the king.” The Pilgrim said, “It is called the Black-Gold Elixir.” Bajie and Sha the Monk snickered to each other in secret. “It is mixed with pot soot—how could it not be black gold?” The officials asked again, “What liquid should be used to take it?” The Pilgrim said, “Either of two medicinal vehicles may be used. The easier one to obtain is a decoction of six things, with which the pills are to be swallowed.” The officials asked, “What are the six things?” The Pilgrim said, “A fart from a crow flying in midair; urine from a carp borne by swift water; face powder used by the Queen Mother; elixir ash from Lord Lao’s furnace; three pieces of a worn-out headcloth once used by the Jade Emperor; and five whiskers from a captive dragon. Decoct those six things and swallow this medicine with the brew, and your king’s melancholy illness will at once be gone.” On hearing this, the officials said, “None of those things exists in the mortal world. May we ask what the other medicinal vehicle is?” The Pilgrim said, “Swallow it with rootless water.” The officials laughed. “That is easy to obtain.” The Pilgrim asked, “How do you know it is easy to obtain?” The officials replied, “Common folk here say that when rootless water is needed, one takes a bowl or cup to a well or river, scoops up some water, then hurries home without setting the vessel down or looking back, and gives it to the patient with the medicine. That is rootless water.” The Pilgrim said, “Water from wells and rivers has roots. The rootless water I mean is nothing of the kind. It is water that falls from heaven and is drunk before touching the ground; only that may be called rootless water.” The officials said again, “That is easy too. We need only wait for a cloudy day when it rains, then have him take the medicine.”

u.src: The officials came to the lodge, prostrated themselves before the Pilgrim, and said, “Our king has specially commanded us to receive the wondrous medicine with due reverence.”
The Pilgrim told Bajie to fetch the box, opened its lid, and handed it to the officials.
The officials respectfully asked, “What is this medicine called?
We should know what to tell the king.”
The Pilgrim said, “It is called the Black-Gold Elixir.”
Bajie and Sha the Monk snickered to each other in secret. “It is mixed with pot soot—how could it not be black gold?”
The officials asked again, “What liquid should be used to take it?”
The Pilgrim said, “Either of two medicinal vehicles may be used.
The easier one to obtain is a decoction of six things, with which the pills are to be swallowed.”
The officials asked, “What are the six things?”

The Pilgrim said, “A fart from a crow flying in midair; urine from a carp borne by swift water; face powder used by the Queen Mother; elixir ash from Lord Lao’s furnace; three pieces of a worn-out headcloth once used by the Jade Emperor; and five whiskers from a captive dragon.
Decoct those six things and swallow this medicine with the brew, and your king’s melancholy illness will at once be gone.”
On hearing this, the officials said, “None of those things exists in the mortal world.
May we ask what the other medicinal vehicle is?”
The Pilgrim said, “Swallow it with rootless water.”
The officials laughed. “That is easy to obtain.”
The Pilgrim asked, “How do you know it is easy to obtain?”

The officials replied, “Common folk here say that when rootless water is needed, one takes a bowl or cup to a well or river, scoops up some water, then hurries home without setting the vessel down or looking back, and gives it to the patient with the medicine. That is rootless water.”
The Pilgrim said, “Water from wells and rivers has roots.
The rootless water I mean is nothing of the kind. It is water that falls from heaven and is drunk before touching the ground; only that may be called rootless water.”
The officials said again, “That is easy too.
We need only wait for a cloudy day when it rains, then have him take the medicine.”

p.src: They bowed their thanks to the Pilgrim and carried the medicine back to present to the king. The king was delighted and immediately ordered an attendant to bring it forward. Looking at it, he asked, “What sort of pills are these?” The officials replied, “The holy monk said they are the ‘Black-Gold Elixir’ and must be swallowed with rootless water.” The king ordered the palace attendants to fetch rootless water. The officials said, “The holy monk told us that rootless water does not come from a well or river; it must fall from heaven and be caught before touching the ground.” The king at once summoned the officer in attendance and issued an edict ordering ritual masters to be invited to pray for rain. The officials obeyed and went out to post the proclamation; of that we shall say no more.

p.src: Now the Pilgrim, in the hall of the Huitong Hostel, called to Zhu Bajie, “Just now I promised him that the medicine could be taken only with water fallen from heaven. In such haste, where are we to find rainwater? This king appears to be a most worthy and virtuous sovereign. How about you and I help bring him a little rain with which to take the medicine?” “How can we help?” asked Bajie. The Pilgrim said, “Stand on my left and serve as the Supporting Star.” Then he called to Sha Wujing, “Stand on my right and serve as the Assisting Constellation. Let old Monkey help him obtain some rootless water.” What a Great Sage! He paced the steps of the Dipper, made the proper hand sign, and recited an incantation. Before long, a black cloud appeared in the due east and gradually drew over his head. A voice called, “Great Sage, Ao Guang, Dragon King of the Eastern Sea, has come to pay his respects.” The Pilgrim said, “I would not dare trouble you without cause. I have asked you here to provide some rootless water with which the king may take his medicine.” The Dragon King replied, “When the Great Sage summoned me, you did not say that water was required. This little dragon has come alone, bringing no rain-making apparatus, nor any wind, cloud, thunder, or lightning. How can I make rain?” The Pilgrim said, “We have no use for wind, cloud, thunder, or lightning now, nor do we need much rain. Just a little water to wash down the medicine will suffice.” The Dragon King said, “If that is all, let me sneeze a couple of times and spit out a little saliva for him to take his medicine with.” Greatly delighted, the Pilgrim said, “Excellent, excellent! Do not delay; set about it at once.”

p.src: The old dragon gradually lowered his black cloud from the sky until it was directly above the imperial palace. Concealing his form, he sprayed out a mouthful of saliva, which at once turned into sweet rain. All the officials at court cheered in unison, “Ten thousand joys to our sovereign! Heaven has sent down blessed rain!” The king immediately issued an edict: “Bring vessels to collect it. Everyone, whether inside or outside the palace and regardless of rank, must await and store this immortal water to save me.” Just look: the civil and military officials, the consorts and concubines of the inner palaces, three thousand palace maids, and eight hundred fair ladies—all raised cups, held goblets, lifted bowls, and carried plates as they waited to catch the blessed rain. The old dragon worked his saliva into rain from midair, never letting it stray beyond the front and rear of the palace. After nearly one double-hour, the Dragon King took leave of the Great Sage and returned to the sea. The ministers gathered in their cups, bowls, and goblets. Some had caught one or two drops, some three or five, and some none at all. Poured together, the water amounted to about three cupfuls, which they presented upon the imperial table. Truly, a wondrous fragrance filled the Golden Throne Hall, and a delicious savor wafted through the sovereign’s court.

p.src: The king took leave of the Master and carried the Black-Gold Elixir and blessed rain into the palace. First he swallowed one pill and drank one cup of rainwater; then he swallowed another pill and drank another cup of blessed rain; and the third time, all three pills had been swallowed and all three cups of blessed rain sent down. Before long, his belly began to rumble incessantly like a turning windlass. A chamber pot was brought at once, and he relieved himself three or five times in succession. After taking a little rice gruel, he lay back upon the dragon bed. Two consorts inspected the chamber pot. Amid indescribable filth and phlegm, they found a lump of glutinous rice. The consorts came beside the dragon bed and reported, “The root of Your Majesty’s illness has all passed out.” The king was greatly pleased to hear this and took another serving of rice gruel.

p.src: After a short while, he gradually felt his chest and heart ease, his vital breath and blood return to harmony, his spirits revive, and strength return to his legs. He got down from the dragon bed, put on his court robes, and immediately ascended the precious hall. On seeing the Tang Monk, he promptly prostrated himself in homage. The elder hastened to return the courtesy. When their bows were finished, the king supported him with his own imperial hand and ordered his chamberlain, “Quickly prepare an invitation, writing upon it the words ‘I bow twice and knock my head,’ and dispatch an officer to respectfully invite the Master’s three eminent disciples. Meanwhile, throw open the Eastern Pavilion and have the Court of Imperial Entertainments arrange a banquet of thanks.” The many officials received the decree: those charged with the invitation prepared it, and those charged with the banquet laid it out. Truly, when a realm exerts its mountain-toppling strength, everything is completed in an instant.

p.src: Now when Bajie saw an official deliver the invitation, he was beside himself with joy. “Brother,” he said, “that truly was marvelous medicine! They have come now to offer thanks, and it is all due to your merit.” Sha Wujing said, “What are you saying, Second Brother? As the common proverb goes, ‘When one man is blessed, the whole household benefits.’ We all helped compound the medicine here, so every one of us has earned merit. Let us simply enjoy ourselves and say no more.” Ah! Just look at the three brothers, all beaming with delight as they went straight into court.

p.src: The king raised a cup with his own imperial hand and first seated the Tang Monk with due honor. Tripitaka said, “This poor monk does not drink wine.” The king said, “It is vegetarian wine. How would it be if the Master drank this one cup?” Tripitaka replied, “Wine is the foremost prohibition of the monastic order.” Feeling deeply apologetic, the king asked, “Since the Master abstains from drink, with what may I show my respect?” Tripitaka said, “Let my three unruly disciples drink in my stead.” Only then was the king delighted. He turned the golden goblet and handed it to the Pilgrim. The Pilgrim accepted it, saluted everyone, and drank a cup. Seeing how readily he drank, the king offered him another cup. The Pilgrim did not refuse, but drank that too. The king laughed and said, “Drink a third cup for the Three Jewels.” Again the Pilgrim did not refuse, but drank it. The king ordered another cup poured, so that he might drink a fourth for the Four Seasons.

p.src: After they had feasted for some time, the king raised another great goblet and offered it to the Pilgrim. The Pilgrim said, “Please be seated, Your Majesty. Old Sun will drink heartily when my turn comes and certainly will not refuse.” The king said, “Holy monk, your kindness is weightier than a mountain, and I can never repay it fully. Please, at all events, drain this great cup, for We have something to tell you.” The Pilgrim said, “Tell me what you have to say, and then Old Sun will drink.” The king said, “For several years I suffered from an illness born of care and suspicion. One dose of your miraculous elixir cleared the obstruction, and thus I recovered.” The Pilgrim laughed. “When Old Sun examined Your Majesty yesterday, I already knew it was an illness caused by anxiety, but I do not know what troubled you so.” The king said, “The ancients said, ‘A family’s shame should not be spoken of outside its doors.’ Yet you, holy monk, are my benefactor. If only you will not laugh, I can tell you.” The Pilgrim said, “How could I dare laugh at you? Pray speak freely.” The king said, “You have come from the East, holy monk. Through how many kingdoms have you passed?” The Pilgrim said, “Five or six.” The king asked again, “What are the queens of those other kingdoms called?” The Pilgrim said, “A king’s queens are called the Chief Consort, the Eastern Consort, and the Western Consort.” The king said, “Our titles are not the same. We call the Chief Consort the Golden Sage Consort, the Eastern Consort the Jade Sage Consort, and the Western Consort the Silver Sage Consort. At present only the Silver and Jade Queens remain in the palace.” The Pilgrim asked, “Why is the Golden Sage Consort not in the palace?” Shedding tears, the king said, “She has been gone for three years.” The Pilgrim asked, “Where did she go?” The king said, “Three years ago, during the Dragon Boat Festival, We and our consorts were beneath the Pomegranate Pavilion in the imperial garden, unwrapping rice dumplings and setting out mugwort, drinking calamus-and-realgar wine, and watching the dragon-boat races. Suddenly a gust of wind arose, and a demon appeared in midair. Calling himself the Great King, Peer of Jupiter, he said that he dwelt in the Xiezhi Cave on Mount Qilin and lacked a wife there. Having learned that my Golden Sage Consort was exquisitely beautiful, he wanted her for his lady and ordered Us to send her out without delay. If she was not presented by his third summons, he would eat Us first, then all our ministers, and finally devour every last commoner in the city. At that moment We feared for our realm and people and had no choice but to send the Golden Sage Consort out beyond the Pomegranate Pavilion. With a single roar, the demon swept her away. The terror of it seized Us, and the rice dumpling We had eaten congealed within our body. Moreover, We grieved and brooded without cease, day and night. Thus this grievous illness lasted three years. Now, after taking your miraculous elixir, holy monk, We have purged several times, expelling nothing but matter that had lain obstructed for those three years. Therefore We now feel sound in body, light in limb, and restored in spirit. My life today is entirely your gift, holy monk. How could your kindness be compared merely to the weight of Mount Tai?”

p.src: Hearing this, the Pilgrim was delighted. He swallowed the great goblet of wine in two draughts, then smiled and asked the king, “So that was the fright and anxiety Your Majesty suffered. Now that you have met Old Sun, you have fortunately recovered. But do you wish the Golden Sage Consort to return to your kingdom?” The king shed tears and said, “We yearn for her without respite, day and night. It is only that no one can subdue the demon. How could We not wish her to return?” The Pilgrim said, “What if Old Sun goes and subdues that evil creature for you?” The king knelt and said, “If you rescue my queen, We will lead the three palace consorts and nine concubines out of the city to become commoners, entrust the whole realm to you, holy monk, and let you reign as emperor.” Watching from the side, Bajie could no longer contain himself when he heard these words and saw this obeisance. He laughed aloud. “This emperor has quite forgotten his dignity! How can he cast away his realm for a wife and kneel before a monk?” The Pilgrim hurried forward, helped the king to his feet, and said, “Your Majesty, since the demon took away the Golden Sage Consort, has he returned at any time?” The king said, “He seized the Golden Sage Consort at the Fifth-Month Festival three years ago. In the tenth month he came demanding two palace maids to attend Her Ladyship, and We surrendered two at once. In the third month of last year he returned and demanded two more palace maids. In the seventh month he took another two. And in the second month of this year he took two more. We do not know when he will come demanding more.” The Pilgrim asked, “Since he comes so often, are you all afraid of him?” The king said, “We have seen him come many times. For one thing, We fear him; for another, We are afraid he may intend us harm. In the fourth month of last year, We ordered craftsmen to construct a Demon-Refuge Tower. Whenever We hear the wind and know he is coming, We take the two queens and nine concubines inside to hide.” The Pilgrim said, “If Your Majesty does not object, how would it be to take Old Sun to inspect this Demon-Refuge Tower?” The king at once took the Pilgrim by his left hand and led him away from the banquet. All the officials rose together. Zhu Bajie said, “Brother, you have no manners. With such imperial wine before us, why break up the banquet and leave our seats to go looking at some tower?” Hearing this, the king understood that Bajie was thinking of his stomach. He ordered the attendants to carry two tables of vegetarian dishes and wine to the Demon-Refuge Tower and wait outside. Only then did the fool cease complaining. He laughed with his master and Sha Monk, saying, “The banquet is moving elsewhere!”

Only then did the fool cease complaining. He laughed with his master and Sha Monk, saying, “The banquet is moving elsewhere!”

p.src: Escorted by the civil and military officials, the king and the Pilgrim walked hand in hand through the imperial palace and into the rear of the imperial garden, where no towers, terraces, halls, or pavilions could be seen. The Pilgrim asked, “Where is the Demon-Refuge Tower?” Before he had finished speaking, two eunuchs appeared carrying two red-lacquered poles and used them to pry up a square stone slab from the open ground. The king said, “It is right here. Beneath us, at a depth of over thirty feet, nine audience chambers have been excavated. Inside are four great vats filled with clear oil, whose lamps burn without cease by day or night. Whenever We hear the wind, We go inside to hide, and people outside cover the entrance with the stone slab.” The Pilgrim laughed. “That demon has no intention of harming you. If he wished to harm you, how could you hide from him here?” As they spoke, a roaring wind suddenly swept in from due south, churning up earth and raising clouds of dust. The officials were so terrified that they all cried resentfully, “This monk has a salt-and-sauce tongue! No sooner does he speak of the demon than the demon arrives!” In panic, the king released the Pilgrim and darted into the underground chamber. The Tang Monk followed him in. Every one of the officials hid themselves away as well.

p.src: When the Pilgrim saw him, he said, “Sandy, do you recognize him?” Sandy replied, “I’ve never met him before. How could I recognize him?” He then asked, “Bajie, do you recognize him?” Bajie replied, “I’ve never shared tea or wine with him, and he’s neither a friend nor a neighbor. How could I recognize him?” The Pilgrim said, “He looks like the Burnt-Faced, Golden-Eyed Ghost who guards the gate under the Great Emperor Equal to Heaven of the Eastern Peak.” “No, no,” said Bajie. The Pilgrim asked, “How do you know it isn’t he?” Bajie replied, “Ghosts are spirits of yin. They do not emerge until the hours of the Monkey, Rooster, Dog, and Boar, from late afternoon into the night. It is still the hour of the Snake today. What ghost would dare come out now? Even if he were a ghost, he could not ride the clouds. Even if he could stir up a wind, it would be no more than a little whirlwind. How could he raise such a raging gale? Perhaps he is the Great King Jupiter’s Rival himself.” The Pilgrim laughed. “You fool! There is some sense in what you say. If that is so, you two stay here and guard the place while I go ask his name. Then I can rescue the Lady of the Golden Sage Palace for the king and bring her back to court.” Bajie said, “Go if you’re going, but whatever you do, don’t give us away.” The Pilgrim proudly made no reply. He hastily mounted his auspicious radiance and sprang upward. Ah! Indeed:
